title: Diving In - Episode 2: Stat tests and my issues with player-focused puzzles in RPGs!
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BfjZU1zyiOc

A direct sequel to the dice episode, built around a comment exchange Daniel (@dungeondive) reads out on camera. A viewer described blaming *themselves* when the dice came up bad, conflating luck with skill. His answer reframes the whole thing: view the game from the character's perspective. It isn't your intelligence being tested, it's theirs. They're the hero; you're there to roll and find out what happens. The viewer's reply — that we are playing fate for the characters we observe — is the line the episode turns on.

From there, the argument against player-focused puzzles. He dislikes GMs handing riddles to players, and the reason is a consistency problem worth sitting with: five minutes before the riddle, your character fought orcs with spells and you did nothing physical. So why is intellect the one stat the player must supply? He follows it to its conclusion — nobody asks players to lift 500lb for a portcullis, sprint 100 metres to escape a trap, or jump a pit the GM dug that afternoon. Mansions of Madness Second Edition is the sympathetic exception, since character stats set your number of attempts, though he cheerfully cheats at the sliding-block puzzles when solo.

A charming illustration comes from a Dungeon Quest video where repeated failures to open a door became, in his reading, a stubborn character — and then a portcullis behind it. Games named for good stat tests: Destinies and Zvijezda's spendable stats, Escape from Dulce, Black Oath's line, Call of Cthulhu's profession-derived skills. Next topic: random encounters.

----

Do you want to solve the riddle yourself, or roll for it? And if you like player-facing puzzles, why should intelligence be tested at the table when strength never is?
